The must-sees

  • Arch of Triumph

    Landmark · 1936

    Earlier wooden arches stood here, and the present one by Petre Antonescu was finished in 1936. It honours the soldiers of the First World War and the union of 1918.

  • Cișmigiu Gardens

    Park

    It was laid out in the mid-19th century around a former pond by the German gardener Carl Meyer. The lake becomes an ice rink in winter.

    Look for: Find the Writers’ Rotunda, where the busts of Romanian authors stand in a ring among the trees.

  • King Michael I Park

    Park

    It was laid out in the 1930s on drained marshland. Long known as Herăstrău Park, it was renamed for King Michael I in 2017.

  • National Museum of Art of Romania

    Museum

    The palace was rebuilt in the 1930s after a fire, and kings Carol II and Michael lived here. Damaged in the fighting of December 1989, it holds Romanian and European art.

    Look for: Opposite stands the Central University Library, which burned in the December 1989 fighting and lost hundreds of thousands of books.

  • National Village Museum

    Museum · 1936

    Sociologist Dimitrie Gusti founded it in 1936. The buildings were brought from villages across Romania and rebuilt here.

    Look for: Find the tall wooden church from Maramureș, with its steep shingled roof and slender spire.

  • Old Town (Lipscani)

    Neighbourhood

    This was the market quarter of the princely capital, and Lipscani Street is named after traders who brought goods from Leipzig. It survived the demolitions of the 1980s and was restored after 2000.

    Look for: Find the ruins of the Old Princely Court, with a bust of Vlad III, the prince later linked to Dracula.

  • Palace of the Parliament

    Civic building

    Ceaușescu began it in 1984 as the House of the People, after a large part of the old quarter was demolished for it. Architect Anca Petrescu led the design, and the National Museum of Contemporary Art now occupies one wing.

    Look for: Look down Union Boulevard from the palace: it is said to have been planned slightly longer than the Champs-Élysées, its model.

  • Revolution Square

    Square

    On 21 December 1989 Ceaușescu’s last speech from the Central Committee balcony turned into protest. The next day he fled from the building’s roof by helicopter.

    Look for: Find the balcony on the long former Central Committee building, now the Interior Ministry, where Ceaușescu stood for his last speech.

  • Romanian Athenaeum

    Culture · 1888

    French architect Albert Galleron designed it, and it opened in 1888. Much of the money came from a public appeal: give a leu for the Athenaeum.

    Look for: Inside the round concert hall, a painted band by Costin Petrescu runs all the way around, telling Romania’s history in scenes.

  • Stavropoleos Monastery

    Church · 1724

    The Greek monk Ioanichie Stratonikeas built it in 1724, with an inn that has since vanished. Today a community of nuns keeps a library of Byzantine music and a choir.

    Look for: In the courtyard arcade, the carved stone crosses and tombstones were rescued from churches demolished elsewhere in the city.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Bucharest and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Bucharest passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
